title: Source-code moats are dead; believers in them are deluding themselves
dek: DHH argues agents drive software development costs to zero. Mac and Windows' mouse-driven interfaces are fundamentally incompatible with agent workflows. Linux's historically criticized features—terminal commands, complex configs, verbose error messages—are exactly what agents need.
why: DHH draws on six months of hands-on experience building Omachi's operating system entirely with agents, covering everything from remapping shortcuts to recreating Lightroom. Dense in examples; for anyone trying to gauge whether AI will reopen the operating-system wars.
who: Founders wondering whether agents will reopen competition in operating systems and desktop markets; engineers and investors writing code with AI and questioning whether a source-code moat still holds.
skip: Skip the opening self-introductions and the closing tangents about offices, nineties demo culture, and dial-up tones—information-light.

points.h: Graphical operating-system settings are fundamentally incompatible with agent workflows
points.body: Remapping Mac workspace shortcuts required manually clicking through settings menus—agents can't batch-configure the way GUIs force. DHH demonstrated letting an agent modify his running macOS directly, and it worked. After five minutes of that experience, he says you can't go back. Mac and Windows' forty years of mouse-click interaction doesn't fit the agent era.

points.h: Linux's historical flaws are exactly what agents want most
points.body: Terminal dependency, complex config files, obscure error messages—Linux's traditional criticisms. DHH sees them as exactly what agents need: command-line interfaces, predictable editable configs, detailed error information. This year's inversion: the historical "flaws" have become reasons to choose Linux if you're working with AI.

points.h: Ecosystem lock-in through scarcity breaks when anyone can code
points.body: An Omachi community member replaced a Mac-only Lightroom dependency by implementing a better version in two weeks—after Adobe spent over a decade and tens of millions developing it. This shows ecosystem lock-in's keystone is crumbling: application availability once locked you in, but now anyone with agent access can generate software in minutes. This resets mobile competition dynamics entirely.

points.h: Token throughput speed determines whether software feels alive
points.body: Omachi currently runs at 50–120 tokens per second—below the threshold for smooth interaction. Fireworks recently demonstrated 1500 tokens per second, generating a playable Tetris in four seconds and reshaping it in real time as DHH shouted modifications. As token throughput scales to hundreds of thousands and millions per second in the coming years, software will become continuously self-rewriting in real time.

points.h: Claiming source code as a moat is now self-delusion
points.body: DHH compares Omachi's development progress over months with the gap between Opus 4.8 and 5.5, noting this pace is accelerating and new models are likely by Christmas or early next year. His conclusion: anyone who thinks source code—even millions of lines—protects their ecosystem is deluding themselves.

points.h: Even unlimited token budgets need only three subscriptions in practice
points.body: After twenty years of building wealth, DHH can afford unlimited token spending. Over three months, only two weeks came close to maxing his quota. Most work runs on a single $200 20X subscription to Claude—frontier models, not open-source alternatives. And he maintains just three subscriptions total. His point: access isn't confined to those with infinite budgets.

points.h: Being in the game matters even when trailing by six months
points.body: DHH acknowledges that open-source models like GLM and DeepSeek likely lag by six or seven months; many benchmarks are suspect anyway, and they may not keep up with Opus in real-world scenarios. But their existence matters: they run locally on your hardware, they preserve competition, and they prevent two labs from owning the market and inflating token prices. Without them, we'd repeat Google and Meta's capture of 99% of internet advertising value.

points.h: Three years to surpass macOS's global installed base is realistic
points.body: Omachi began last year as DHH's hand-written bash-script hobby—just better computers for him and a few friends. With agents, his ambition exploded: beat macOS globally within three years—180 million total users, which doesn't even rank as a tier-C internet service. He even questions whether twelve months is feasible; his reasoning: if labs truly believe recursive self-improving AI arrives within twelve months, an OS's market share should be surmountable.
